topic: Euler’s Identity: The Most Beautiful Equation
target_audience: University students (Engineering/Math majors) or advanced high school students

outline.topic: Euler’s Identity: The Most Beautiful Equation
outline.target_audience: University students (Engineering/Math majors) or advanced high school students

sections.title: Introduction: Bridging the Worlds
sections.content: Hook the audience by connecting three seemingly unrelated constants: 'e' (growth), 'i' (rotation), and 'π' (geometry). Introduce the goal: to show how they unify into e^(πi) + 1 = 0.
sections.example: A spinning mechanical gear moving along a circular path in the complex plane.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Complex Plane
sections.content: Visualize complex numbers as coordinates (a, b) on a plane. Explain 'i' not as an imaginary concept, but as a 90-degree counter-clockwise rotation operator.
sections.example: A squirrel on a Cartesian grid jumping 90 degrees left whenever it encounters 'i'.

sections.title: The Growth Factor: e and Circular Motion
sections.content: Introduce e^x as exponential growth. Explain that e^(it) forces growth to move at a right angle to the current position, creating a circular trajectory rather than a straight line.
sections.example: An arrow moving forward (growth) that is constantly pulled sideways by a magnet, forcing it into a circle.

sections.title: Deriving Euler’s Formula
sections.content: Present Euler’s Formula: e^(ix) = cos(x) + i*sin(x). Use an animation of a vector rotating around the unit circle to show how its real and imaginary parts map to cosine and sine functions.
sections.example: A satellite orbiting a central planet, where its position at any time t is defined by (cos t, sin t).

sections.title: The Finale: Substituting π
sections.content: Substitute x = π into the formula. Since cos(π) = -1 and sin(π) = 0, the equation collapses to e^(πi) = -1. Emphasize the elegance of this connection.
sections.example: The 'orbiting satellite' completes exactly half a rotation to land on the negative real axis at -1.

storyboard.title: Introduction: Bridging the Worlds
lecture_lines: e, i, and pi bridge separate math worlds.
animations: Fade in text 'Introduction to the Complex Universe'. #FFFFFF
Draw axes representing the Real and Imaginary components. #FF00FF
Animate a point rotating around the unit circle. #00FFFF
Label the point as 'z' with a tracking vector. #FFFF00
Highlight the identity e^iθ = cosθ + i sinθ. #FF0000

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Complex Plane
lecture_lines: Complex numbers sit on a plane.
Multiplying by i rotates ninety degrees.
animations: Show the complex plane with Real and Imaginary axes. #FFFFFF
Draw a vector from the origin to (1, 1). #0000FF

storyboard.title: The Growth Factor: e and Circular Motion
lecture_lines: e to the x is growth.
e to the it grows sideways.
This force creates a circular path.
animations: Represent growth using the base constant e. #FF9900
Illustrate rotational velocity as circular motion. #FF00FF
Show the link between exponential growth and rotation. #00FFFF

storyboard.title: Deriving Euler’s Formula
lecture_lines: Euler's formula links exponentials to circles.
e to the ix equals cos(x) plus i sin(x).
A rotating vector maps these parts.
animations: Display the Taylor series expansion for e^x. #FFFFFF
Substitute x with iθ in the series. #FFFF00
Separate real and imaginary terms of the series. #00FF00
Identify the series for cos(θ) and sin(θ). #FF0000
Finalize the equation: e^iθ = cosθ + i sinθ. #FFFFFF

storyboard.title: The Finale: Substituting π
lecture_lines: Let us set x to pi.
This gives e to the pi i.
animations: Set the angle θ to π radians. #FFFFFF
Simplify the full expression to e^iπ + 1 = 0. #FF0000
